name: Linear Algebra
description: Authored computational and reasoning practice across the supplied lecture syllabus, from linear systems and transformations to eigenstructure, discrete dynamics, orthogonality, least squares and the spectral theorem. Matrices are written as lists of rows and vectors as coordinate tuples; scalars are real unless a problem explicitly uses complex numbers.
limitations: Scope follows the supplied local lecture transcription and overview, not a live verification of the 2026-27 syllabus. Historical assessment and grading rules vary between supplied documents and are omitted.

Text extraction was attempted for all 21 lecture PDFs, which are predominantly image-based. Only representative PDF pages were visually sampled; the supplied Lectures.md transcription is the main content source and can contain OCR errors.
Selected 2023 exam solutions and supplementary notes were sampled, not the complete examination archive or textbook. Video recordings and external links were not reviewed.

QR factorization is explicitly excluded in the supplied lecture 18 programme and is not taught here. This is a full lecture-theme practice set, not a claim to reproduce every textbook section or official exercise.
Problems and explanations are newly authored. Source links identify conceptual grounding rather than official question provenance or an official marking scheme.
Open responses are ungraded and require human review using their rubrics. The portable file does not integrate with the application or implement a grader.

sources.locator: Lectures 1-2: linear systems, echelon forms, linear combinations, spans and matrix equations
Lectures 3-4: homogeneous systems, independence, linear transformations and standard matrices
Lectures 5-6: matrix arithmetic, transpose, inverse matrices and invertible matrix theorem
Lectures 8-9: subspaces, null and column spaces, bases, coordinates, dimension and rank theorem
Lecture 10: cofactor expansion, row operations and determinant identities
Lectures 11-12: eigenvalues, eigenspaces, algebraic/geometric multiplicity, similarity and diagonalization
Lectures 13-14: complex eigenpairs, real scale-rotation blocks and discrete dynamical systems
Lectures 15-16: inner products, orthogonal complements, orthogonal matrices and projections
Lectures 18-19: Gram-Schmidt without QR factorization, least-squares solutions, normal equations and linear models
Lecture 20: real symmetric matrices, orthogonal diagonalization and spectral theorem
Lectures 7 and 17: direct proofs, contradiction and verified counterexamples
Course learning objectives and schedule; historical code CSE1205
Pages 1-3: sampled computational and academic-reasoning formats; no questions copied

topics.name: Linear systems, echelon forms and spans
topics.description: Translate equations into matrices and interpret pivots, consistency and linear combinations.

skills.name: Solve and classify systems
skills.description: Use reversible row operations and identify inconsistent rows and free variables.

skills.name: Vector and matrix equations
skills.description: Translate Ax=b into a linear combination of columns and test span membership.

lesson.title: Row operations preserve the solution set
paragraphs: A linear system becomes an augmented matrix by storing coefficients and then the right-hand side. Swapping rows, multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar, and adding a multiple of one row to another preserve its solutions. Never apply a row operation only to coefficients while leaving the right-hand side unchanged.
For x+y=5 and 2x-y=1, subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives -3y=-9. Back substitution yields y=3 and x=2. A row [0,0|4] would instead say 0=4 and make the system inconsistent.

In echelon form, each leading entry lies to the right of the one above and all-zero rows are at the bottom. Reduced echelon form additionally makes every pivot 1 and the only nonzero entry in its column. A consistent system has a unique solution exactly when every variable is a pivot variable; otherwise there are infinitely many real solutions.

lesson.title: Columns explain multiplication
paragraphs: If A has columns a_1,...,a_n, then Ax=x_1 a_1+...+x_n a_n. Therefore Ax=b is solvable exactly when b belongs to the span of the columns. The augmented column is a target vector, not another unknown.

For columns (1,0,1) and (0,1,1), a combination with coefficients s,t is (s,t,s+t). Their span is the plane z=x+y. Thus (2,3,5) belongs with coefficients 2,3, but (2,3,6) does not. A geometric constraint often explains inconsistency more clearly than a long elimination.

exercises.title: Eliminate one variable
exercises.prompt: Solve x+y=7 and 2x-y=2. Give x.
exercises.explanation: Adding the equations gives 3x=9, hence x=3 and y=4.

exercises.title: Back substitution
exercises.prompt: Solve x+2y-z=1, y+3z=7, z=2. Give x.
exercises.explanation: From z=2 obtain y=1, then x+2-2=1 gives x=1.

exercises.title: Recognize inconsistency
exercises.prompt: An augmented matrix reduces to rows [1,2|3] and [0,0|1]. How many solutions does the system have?
exercises.explanation: The second row represents 0=1. No assignment can satisfy it.

exercises.title: Parametric solution set
exercises.prompt: Describe all solutions of x+2y-z=4 and y+z=1 as a vector plus a scalar multiple of a vector.
exercises.explanation: Set z=t. Then y=1-t and x=2+3t, so (x,y,z)=(2,1,0)+t(3,-1,1), t real.

exercises.title: A consistency parameter
exercises.prompt: For which k is x+2y=3, 2x+4y=k consistent?
exercises.explanation: The second left-hand side is twice the first, so its right-hand side must be twice 3.

exercises.title: Reduced or only echelon?
exercises.prompt: Is [[1,2,0],[0,1,3],[0,0,0]] in reduced row echelon form? Explain.
exercises.explanation: It is in echelon form but not reduced form: the pivot in column 2 has a nonzero entry 2 above it. Replacing row 1 by row 1 minus twice row 2 fixes that column.

exercises.title: Matrix-vector entry
exercises.prompt: For A=[[1,2,-1],[0,3,4]] and v=(2,-1,3), find the second entry of Av.
exercises.explanation: The second row gives 0*2+3*(-1)+4*3=9.

exercises.title: Membership in a span
exercises.prompt: Is (3,4,7) in span{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}? Give coefficients or explain why not.

exercises.title: A vector outside the column space
exercises.prompt: Explain why (1,2,4) is not a linear combination of (1,0,1) and (0,1,1).
exercises.explanation: Any combination is (s,t,s+t). The first two entries force s=1,t=2, but then the third is 3 rather than 4.
rubric: Use the first coordinates to force coefficients.

exercises.title: Surjectivity from pivots
exercises.prompt: A 3 by 5 matrix has a pivot in every row. Is Ax=b solvable for every b in R^3? Explain the column-span connection.
exercises.explanation: Yes. A pivot in every row means the columns span R^3, so every b is a column combination. There are two free variables, so each such system has infinitely many solutions.
rubric: Connect row pivots to spanning the codomain.
Distinguish existence for every b from uniqueness.

topics.name: Independence and linear transformations
topics.description: Relate homogeneous solutions to independence and build transformations from basis images.

skills.name: Linear independence
skills.description: Analyze zero combinations and homogeneous solution sets.

skills.name: Linear maps
skills.description: Check linearity, assemble standard matrices and reason about composition and injectivity.

lesson.title: The homogeneous system tests independence
paragraphs: Vectors v_1,...,v_n are independent when c_1 v_1+...+c_n v_n=0 forces every coefficient to be zero. With the vectors as matrix columns, this is exactly the question whether Ax=0 has only its trivial solution. Any free variable produces a nontrivial dependence.

For v_1=(1,0), v_2=(0,1), v_3=(1,1), the relation v_1+v_2-v_3=0 proves dependence. All three vectors are nonzero, showing why nonzero vectors need not be independent. In R^m, any set of more than m vectors is dependent.

When Ax=b is consistent and p is one particular solution, all solutions are p+z with z in Nul(A). Subtracting any two solutions gives a homogeneous solution, which explains the common direction vectors of parallel affine solution sets.

lesson.title: A linear map is fixed by basis images
paragraphs: Linearity means T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v) for all vectors and scalars. It implies T(0)=0; this gives a quick disproof for a translation, but T(0)=0 alone does not prove linearity. Squaring each coordinate also sends zero to zero and still fails additivity.

The standard matrix of T:R^n to R^m has columns T(e_1),...,T(e_n). For T(x,y)=(x-2y,3x), it is [[1,-2],[3,0]]. A composition S after T has matrix BA when T has matrix A and S has matrix B: the rightmost operation acts first.

A linear map is one-to-one exactly when its kernel is {0}, equivalently a pivot in every matrix column. It is onto its stated codomain exactly when there is a pivot in every row. Rectangular maps make these distinct conditions visible.

exercises.title: Independent pair
exercises.prompt: Are (1,2) and (2,5) linearly independent? Show a zero-combination argument.
exercises.explanation: If a+2b=0 and 2a+5b=0, subtracting twice the first from the second gives b=0, then a=0. Thus the pair is independent.
rubric: Set a linear combination equal to zero.

exercises.title: An explicit dependence
exercises.prompt: Find a nontrivial dependence among u=(1,1,0), v=(0,1,1), w=(1,2,1).
exercises.explanation: u+v=w, so u+v-w=0 with coefficients (1,1,-1), not all zero.

exercises.title: Dimension obstruction
exercises.prompt: Can five vectors in R^4 be linearly independent?

options.text: Yes, if all five are nonzero
No, a 4 by 5 matrix must have a free variable

exercises.explanation: There can be at most four pivots in a 4 by 5 matrix, leaving a nontrivial homogeneous solution and hence a dependence.

exercises.title: Particular plus homogeneous
exercises.prompt: For A=[[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] and b=(3,4), describe all x satisfying Ax=b.
exercises.explanation: Taking x2=t gives x1=3-t and x3=4-t. Hence x=(3,0,4)+t(-1,1,-1). The first vector maps to b and the direction maps to zero.
rubric: Provide a particular solution and null direction.
Show the parameter covers every solution.

exercises.title: Build a standard matrix
exercises.prompt: Find the standard matrix for T(x,y)=(2x-y,x+3y,4y).

exercises.title: Reject a translation
exercises.prompt: Is T(x,y)=(x+1,y) linear? Give a decisive counterexample.
exercises.explanation: No. T(0,0)=(1,0), whereas every linear map must send zero to zero.

exercises.title: Composition order
exercises.prompt: Let R rotate R^2 counterclockwise by 90 degrees and F reflect across the x-axis. Find the standard matrix of F after R.
exercises.explanation: R(x,y)=(-y,x), followed by F gives (-y,-x). The matrix is [[0,-1],[-1,0]], obtained as FR.
rubric: Form the resulting columns or matrix product in the correct order.

exercises.title: Injective rectangular map
exercises.prompt: For T(x,y)=(x,y,x+y), determine whether T:R^2 to R^3 is one-to-one and whether it is onto.
exercises.explanation: Its kernel is zero, so it is one-to-one. Its outputs obey z=x+y, so it is not onto R^3; for example (0,0,1) is unreachable.
rubric: Give a range restriction or unreachable vector.

exercises.title: Use supplied basis images
exercises.prompt: A linear T satisfies T(1,0)=(2,1) and T(0,1)=(-1,3). Find the first coordinate of T(3,2).

exercises.title: Kernel of a transformation
exercises.prompt: Find a basis for the kernel of T(x,y,z)=(x+y,y+z).
exercises.explanation: The kernel equations give x=-y,z=-y. Thus the kernel is span{(-1,1,-1)}, and that single nonzero vector is a basis.
rubric: Give a basis rather than only a set of equations.

topics.name: Matrix operations and invertibility
topics.description: Respect dimensions and multiplication order while using inverse identities.

skills.name: Matrix algebra
skills.description: Compute products, transpose expressions and solve ordered matrix equations.

skills.name: Inverses and equivalences
skills.description: Find inverses and apply the invertible matrix theorem for square matrices.

lesson.title: Order and dimensions carry meaning
paragraphs: The product of an m by n matrix and an n by p matrix is m by p. Its (i,j) entry is row i of the first matrix dotted with column j of the second. Matrix multiplication describes composition, so exchanging the factors generally changes the transformation.

Transposition reverses multiplication: (AB)^T=B^T A^T. Inverses also reverse multiplication: (AB)^(-1)=B^(-1)A^(-1), when both inverses exist. Verify such identities by multiplying and cancelling adjacent inverse pairs, never by commuting unrelated factors.

lesson.title: An inverse undoes a bijective map
paragraphs: A square matrix A is invertible when a matrix A^(-1) satisfies both inverse identities. Reduce [A|I] to [I|A^(-1)] using complete row operations. For [[2,1],[1,1]], the inverse is [[1,-1],[-1,2]]; direct multiplication yields I.

For an n by n matrix, invertibility, n pivots, independent columns, columns spanning R^n, unique solvability of Ax=b for every b, and a trivial null space are equivalent. These square-matrix equivalences should not be transferred without modification to rectangular matrices.

To solve AXB=C with invertible A and B, multiply on the left by A^(-1) and on the right by B^(-1): X=A^(-1)CB^(-1). Placement matters. A zero matrix product does not in general force a zero factor because singular maps can send the range of another map to zero.

exercises.title: A product entry
exercises.explanation: Row 2 of A dotted with column 2 of B gives 3*0+4*5=20.

exercises.title: Product dimensions
exercises.prompt: A is 2 by 3 and B is 3 by 4. Which statement is correct?

options.text: AB is 2 by 4; BA is undefined
AB is 3 by 3; BA is 4 by 2

exercises.explanation: The inner dimensions match for AB but not for BA, whose inner dimensions would be 4 and 2.

exercises.title: Noncommutativity by example
exercises.prompt: For A=[[0,1],[0,0]] and B=[[0,0],[1,0]], compute AB and BA and explain what they show.
exercises.explanation: AB=[[1,0],[0,0]], whereas BA=[[0,0],[0,1]]. They differ, disproving commutativity of matrix multiplication in general.

exercises.title: Transpose of a triple product
exercises.prompt: Rewrite (ABC)^T in terms of A^T, B^T and C^T.
exercises.explanation: (ABC)^T=C^T B^T A^T. Applying the two-factor transpose identity twice reverses the order of all three factors.

exercises.title: Solve a matrix equation
exercises.prompt: For invertible square A and B, solve AXB=C for X.
exercises.explanation: Multiply first on the left by A^(-1), then on the right by B^(-1), giving X=A^(-1)CB^(-1).
rubric: Apply inverse factors on their correct sides.

exercises.title: Two-by-two inverse
exercises.prompt: Find the inverse of [[3,2],[1,1]] and verify it by multiplication.
exercises.explanation: The inverse is [[1,-2],[-1,3]]. Multiplying gives [[3-2,-6+6],[1-1,-2+3]]=I.

exercises.title: Solve using inverse data
exercises.prompt: A^(-1)=[[2,-1],[0,1]]. For Ax=(4,3), find the first coordinate of x.
exercises.explanation: x=A^(-1)b, so its first coordinate is 2*4-3=5.

exercises.title: Singular parameter
exercises.prompt: For which real t is [[1,t],[2,6]] not invertible?
exercises.explanation: Subtracting twice row 1 from row 2 gives [0,6-2t]. A pivot is lost exactly at t=3.

exercises.title: Inverse of a product proof
exercises.prompt: Prove (AB)^(-1)=B^(-1)A^(-1) for invertible square A and B.
exercises.explanation: (AB)(B^(-1)A^(-1))=A I A^(-1)=I, and (B^(-1)A^(-1))(AB)=B^(-1) I B=I. Thus the proposed matrix is a two-sided inverse.

exercises.title: Zero product with nonzero factors
exercises.prompt: Construct two nonzero 2 by 2 real matrices A,B with AB=0.
exercises.explanation: Take A=[[1,0],[0,0]] and B=[[0,0],[0,1]]. Both are nonzero and their product is the zero matrix.
rubric: Verify every product entry is zero.

topics.name: Subspaces, bases and coordinates
topics.description: Identify linear spaces, build bases and apply rank-nullity with the correct ambient dimension.

skills.name: Subspaces and bases
skills.description: Check closure and extract null-space and column-space bases.

skills.name: Coordinates and dimension
skills.description: Solve coordinate equations and use rank-nullity and dimension constraints.

lesson.title: Subspaces contain every linear combination
paragraphs: A nonempty subset is a subspace if it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. In particular it must contain zero. The plane x+y+z=0 is a subspace; the parallel plane x+y+z=1 is not. A null space is always a subspace because A(au+bv)=aAu+bAv.

A basis both spans and is independent. To find a null-space basis, row reduce Ax=0 and assign each free variable in turn to 1 with the others 0. To find a column-space basis, locate pivot columns in the reduced matrix but select the corresponding columns of the original matrix: row operations can move the column space.

lesson.title: Coordinates depend on an ordered basis
paragraphs: For B=(b_1,...,b_k), the coordinate vector [v]_B lists coefficients in v=c_1 b_1+...+c_k b_k. With b_1=(1,1),b_2=(1,-1), the vector (5,1) has coordinates (3,2), since 3b_1+2b_2=(5,1). Coordinates and ordinary entries need not match.

For an m by n matrix, rank(A)+dim Nul(A)=n, the number of columns. The rank is also the dimension of the column space, a subspace of R^m. For a rank-3 matrix with seven columns, nullity is four regardless of its number of rows.

In a k-dimensional space, k independent vectors form a basis, and k spanning vectors form a basis. Fewer than k vectors cannot span it and more than k cannot be independent. These facts let a dimension count replace unnecessary elimination, once membership is established.

exercises.title: A homogeneous plane
exercises.prompt: Show that W={(x,y,z):x-2y+z=0} is a subspace and give a basis.
exercises.explanation: It is the null space of [1,-2,1], hence a subspace. Set y=s,z=t, giving (x,y,z)=s(2,1,0)+t(-1,0,1). These two vectors are independent and form a basis.
rubric: Parametrize with two independent spanning vectors.

exercises.title: An affine plane fails
exercises.prompt: Is {(x,y,z):x+y+z=2} a subspace of R^3? Explain.
exercises.explanation: No. It excludes (0,0,0), which satisfies x+y+z=0 rather than 2. Every subspace contains zero.
rubric: Connect the failure to the subspace definition.

exercises.title: Null-space basis
exercises.prompt: Find a basis of the null space of A=[[1,2,0,-1],[0,0,1,3]].
exercises.explanation: Let x2=s,x4=t. Then x1=-2s+t and x3=-3t. A basis is {(-2,1,0,0),(1,0,-3,1)}.
rubric: Give independent direction vectors satisfying Ax=0.

exercises.title: Original pivot columns
exercises.prompt: A=[[1,2,0],[2,4,1],[0,0,1]] has pivot columns 1 and 3 after row reduction. Give a basis for Col(A).
exercises.explanation: Use columns 1 and 3 of the original A: (1,2,0) and (0,1,1). They are independent and column 2 is twice column 1.
rubric: Explain their independence and spanning property.

exercises.title: Coordinates in a new basis
exercises.prompt: For ordered basis B=((1,1),(1,-1)), find the first coordinate of (7,1) relative to B.
exercises.explanation: Solve c1+c2=7 and c1-c2=1. Then c1=4,c2=3.

exercises.title: Recover the vector
exercises.prompt: B=((1,0,1),(0,1,1)) is a basis of W. If [v]_B=(2,-3), find v.
rubric: Use coordinate entries as coefficients of basis vectors.

exercises.title: Rank-nullity
exercises.prompt: A is a 4 by 7 matrix of rank 3. Find dim Nul(A).
exercises.explanation: Rank plus nullity equals the number of columns, so nullity is 7-3=4.

exercises.title: Complete a basis
exercises.prompt: Give a vector that completes (1,0,1),(0,1,1) to a basis of R^3, and justify it.
exercises.explanation: Choose (0,0,1). A zero combination gives its first two coefficients zero from the first two coordinates, then its third coefficient zero. Hence all three vectors are independent.
rubric: Choose a vector outside the existing span.

exercises.title: Intersection of two planes
exercises.prompt: Find a basis for the intersection of x+y+z=0 and x-y=0 in R^3.
exercises.explanation: x=y=t and z=-2t, so the intersection is span{(1,1,-2)}.

exercises.title: A union is not generally a subspace
exercises.prompt: Use the two coordinate axes in R^2 to show that the union of two subspaces need not be a subspace.
exercises.explanation: The x-axis and y-axis are subspaces. Their union contains (1,0) and (0,1), but not their sum (1,1), so it fails closure under addition.
rubric: Exhibit two union members whose sum leaves the union.

topics.name: Determinants and row operations
topics.description: Compute efficiently and track how elementary operations change determinant values.

skills.name: Compute determinants
skills.description: Use triangular structure, cofactors and elimination with sign tracking.

skills.name: Determinant identities
skills.description: Apply multiplicative, transpose, inverse and scaling rules.

lesson.title: A scalar summary of a square map
paragraphs: For [[a,b],[c,d]], the determinant is ad-bc. A triangular matrix has determinant equal to the product of diagonal entries. A zero determinant means a square matrix is singular; a nonzero determinant means its columns form a basis of the entire codomain.
Cofactor expansion across row i sums a_ij(-1)^(i+j)det(M_ij). Choosing a row or column with many zeros saves work. For [[2,0,0],[1,3,4],[5,6,7]], expansion along the first row gives 2(21-24)=-6.

A row swap changes the determinant sign. Multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k. Adding a multiple of one row to another preserves it. These rules allow elimination, but the determinant of the final triangular matrix must be corrected for swaps and scalings.

lesson.title: Useful identities and tempting false ones
paragraphs: For square matrices of the same size, det(AB)=det(A)det(B), det(A^T)=det(A), and det(A^(-1))=1/det(A) when A is invertible. Multiplying an n by n matrix by k scales every row, so det(kA)=k^n det(A), not k det(A).

There is no general rule det(A+B)=det(A)+det(B). Taking A=B=I_2 yields det(A+B)=4 but det(A)+det(B)=2. Determinants are linear in one row while the other rows are fixed; that is a different statement from linearity in the whole matrix.

exercises.title: Basic determinant
exercises.explanation: The determinant is 4*5-3*2=14.

exercises.title: Triangular structure
exercises.explanation: The upper-triangular determinant is the diagonal product 2*(-3)*5=-30.

exercises.title: Sparse cofactor expansion
exercises.explanation: Expand across row 1. The only contribution is -2 det([[1,4],[0,6]])=-12.

exercises.title: Track three operations
exercises.prompt: det(A)=5. Obtain B by swapping two rows, multiplying one row by 3, and then adding four times another row to it. Find det(B).
exercises.explanation: The swap contributes -1, the scaling contributes 3 and row addition contributes 1. Thus det(B)=-1*3*5=-15.

exercises.title: Scale a three-by-three matrix
exercises.prompt: A is 3 by 3 with det(A)=-2. Find det(2A).
exercises.explanation: Scaling all three rows by 2 multiplies the determinant by 2^3=8, giving -16.

exercises.title: Product and inverse
exercises.prompt: For invertible 2 by 2 matrices with det(A)=2 and det(B)=3, find det(A^(-1)B^2). Give an exact fraction.
exercises.explanation: Multiplicativity and the inverse identity give (1/2)*3^2=9/2.
rubric: Square the determinant of B and multiply.

exercises.title: Find singular values of a parameter
exercises.prompt: For which real t is [[t,1],[4,t]] singular?
exercises.explanation: The determinant is t^2-4, so the singular parameters are t=2 and t=-2.

exercises.title: Refute additivity
exercises.prompt: Give a concrete counterexample to det(A+B)=det(A)+det(B) for 2 by 2 matrices.
exercises.explanation: Let A=B=I_2. Then det(A+B)=det(2I_2)=4, while det(A)+det(B)=2.
rubric: Compute unequal sides of the proposed identity.

exercises.title: Dependent rows
exercises.prompt: What is the determinant of [[1,2,3],[2,4,6],[0,1,1]]?
exercises.explanation: Row 2 is twice row 1. Subtracting twice row 1 creates a zero row without changing the determinant, so it is zero.

exercises.title: Transpose and product
exercises.prompt: A is square and det(A)=3. Find det(A^T A).
exercises.explanation: det(A^T A)=det(A^T)det(A)=det(A)^2=9.

topics.name: Eigenvalues, similarity and diagonalization
topics.description: Compute eigenspaces and separate repeated eigenvalues from insufficient eigenvectors.

skills.name: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces
skills.description: Solve characteristic equations and homogeneous eigenvector equations.

skills.name: Diagonalization and similarity
skills.description: Assemble matching eigenbases, inspect multiplicities and compute matrix powers.

lesson.title: Eigenvectors keep their direction
paragraphs: An eigenvector is a nonzero v satisfying Av=lambda v. The zero vector belongs to every eigenspace but is never an eigenvector. Solve det(A-lambda I)=0 for candidate eigenvalues and then solve (A-lambda I)v=0 for their eigenspaces.

For [[2,1],[0,3]], the eigenvalues are 2 and 3. For 2 the eigenspace is span{(1,0)}; for 3 it is span{(1,1)}. Distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors. Their basis matrix P=[[1,1],[0,1]] and D=diag(2,3) satisfy AP=PD and A=PDP^(-1).

lesson.title: Count eigenvectors, not just roots
paragraphs: Algebraic multiplicity counts a root's repetitions in the characteristic polynomial; geometric multiplicity is the dimension of its eigenspace. Diagonalization needs enough independent eigenvectors to form a basis. For [[2,1],[0,2]], the sole eigenvalue 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2 but only one independent eigenvector, so it is not diagonalizable.

A repeated eigenvalue does not automatically prevent diagonalization: 2I has an entire two-dimensional eigenspace. Conversely, a matrix with n distinct real eigenvalues is diagonalizable over the reals. The scalar field matters when eigenvalues are nonreal.

Similar matrices A=PBP^(-1) represent the same map in different bases and share their characteristic polynomial. Powers simplify as A^k=PD^kP^(-1) after diagonalization. Row-equivalent matrices need not share eigenvalues; row operations preserve solution relationships, not similarity.

exercises.title: Verify an eigenvector
exercises.prompt: For A=[[4,1],[2,3]] and v=(1,1), find the corresponding eigenvalue.

exercises.title: Solve a characteristic equation
exercises.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of A=[[2,1],[1,2]].
exercises.explanation: det(A-lambda I)=(2-lambda)^2-1=(lambda-1)(lambda-3). The eigenvalues are 1 and 3.

exercises.title: An eigenspace basis
exercises.prompt: Find a basis of the eigenspace for eigenvalue 2 of A=[[2,1],[0,3]].
exercises.explanation: A-2I=[[0,1],[0,1]], so y=0 and x is free. The eigenspace is span{(1,0)}.

exercises.title: A defective matrix
exercises.prompt: Is [[4,1],[0,4]] diagonalizable over R? Explain using multiplicities.
exercises.explanation: The only eigenvalue is 4 with algebraic multiplicity 2. Its eigenspace consists of (x,0), dimension 1. There is no basis of eigenvectors, so it is not diagonalizable.
rubric: Compare it with the algebraic multiplicity.

exercises.title: Repeated but diagonalizable
exercises.prompt: Does a repeated eigenvalue force a real matrix to be non-diagonalizable?

options.text: Only when the eigenvalue is positive

exercises.explanation: 3I_2 has eigenvalue 3 twice but two independent eigenvectors, indeed every nonzero vector is an eigenvector.

exercises.title: Construct a diagonalization
exercises.prompt: Diagonalize A=[[1,2],[0,3]] over R by giving P,D and checking AP=PD.
exercises.explanation: Choose eigenvectors (1,0) for 1 and (1,1) for 3. P=[[1,1],[0,1]], D=diag(1,3); both AP and PD equal [[1,3],[0,3]]. P is invertible, so A=PDP^(-1).
rubric: Match each diagonal entry to the corresponding eigenvector column.
Check AP=PD and invertibility of P.

exercises.title: Power on an eigenvector
exercises.prompt: If Av=3v for nonzero v, what scalar c satisfies A^4v=cv?
exercises.explanation: Repeated application gives A^4v=3^4v=81v.

exercises.title: Similarity transfers eigenvectors
exercises.prompt: Suppose A=PBP^(-1), P is invertible, and Bv=lambda v with v nonzero. Prove Pv is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue lambda.
exercises.explanation: A(Pv)=PBv=lambda Pv. Invertibility of P ensures Pv!=0, completing the eigenvector definition.

exercises.title: Zero eigenvalue and invertibility
exercises.prompt: A 4 by 4 matrix has zero as an eigenvalue. What is its determinant?
exercises.explanation: There is nonzero v with Av=0, so A is singular and det(A)=0.

exercises.title: A matrix-power formula
exercises.prompt: For A=[[2,1],[0,3]], derive A^k for integers k>=0 using its eigenbasis.
exercises.explanation: With P=[[1,1],[0,1]], D=diag(2,3), P^(-1)=[[1,-1],[0,1]], multiplication gives A^k=[[2^k,3^k-2^k],[0,3^k]]. It also yields I at k=0.
rubric: Compute the off-diagonal entry and include k=0.

topics.name: Complex eigenvalues and discrete dynamics
topics.description: Interpret nonreal eigenpairs and determine long-term behavior from invariant directions.

skills.name: Complex eigenstructure
skills.description: Find conjugate pairs and relate them to real scale-rotation matrices.

skills.name: Discrete trajectories
skills.description: Expand initial conditions in eigenvectors and classify growth, decay and neutral modes.

lesson.title: Complex values describe real rotations
paragraphs: A real matrix can have nonreal eigenvalues, which occur in conjugate pairs. For R=[[0,-1],[1,0]], the characteristic equation is lambda^2+1=0, so the eigenvalues are i and -i. There are no nonzero real eigenvectors: a quarter turn has no preserved real line direction.

A block C=[[a,-b],[b,a]] acts like multiplication by a+bi. Write a+bi=r exp(i theta), then C is a rotation by theta followed by uniform scaling by r=sqrt(a^2+b^2). Its kth power scales by r^k and rotates by k theta.

If Av=(a-bi)v for a real matrix A and b nonzero, write v=p+iq. Comparing real and imaginary parts gives Ap=ap+bq and Aq=-bp+aq. With P=[p,q] and C=[[a,-b],[b,a]], this yields AP=PC on the invariant plane spanned by p and q. If A is 2 by 2, p and q form a real basis, so P is invertible and A=PCP^(-1). For larger A, P is rectangular and this inverse formula does not apply. Using the other conjugate eigenvector reverses a sign convention, so always verify AP=PC.

lesson.title: Eigenmodes evolve separately
paragraphs: For x_(k+1)=Ax_k, the state is A^k x_0. If v_j form an eigenbasis and x_0=sum c_j v_j, then x_k=sum c_j lambda_j^k v_j. Modes with |lambda|<1 decay; modes with |lambda|>1 grow unless their initial coefficient vanishes.

A negative eigenvalue causes alternating signs. A mode with lambda=1 remains fixed, and lambda=-1 usually oscillates without decay. Thus merely having no eigenvalue larger than 1 numerically is insufficient; modulus matters. Boundary cases on the unit circle require care, especially when a matrix is not diagonalizable.

For diag(1,1/2), every trajectory tends to its initial first-coordinate component on the fixed axis. The origin is not an attractor for all starting points. For diag(2,1/2), one direction expands and the other contracts, making the origin a saddle.

exercises.title: Quarter-turn eigenvalues
exercises.prompt: Find the eigenvalues over C of [[0,-1],[1,0]] and explain why it is not diagonalizable over R.
exercises.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is lambda^2+1, with roots i,-i. A real diagonalization would give real eigenvalues, impossible here. Over C the distinct eigenvalues do permit diagonalization.
rubric: Distinguish the real and complex fields.

exercises.title: Check a complex eigenvector
exercises.prompt: For R=[[0,-1],[1,0]], verify that v=(1,-i) has eigenvalue i.
exercises.explanation: Rv=(i,1), while iv=(i,-i^2)=(i,1). The vector is nonzero, so the eigenpair is valid.

exercises.title: Scale factor from a complex block
exercises.prompt: For C=[[3,-4],[4,3]], by what positive factor does C multiply the Euclidean norm of every vector?
exercises.explanation: C corresponds to 3+4i, whose modulus is 5. Equivalently C^T C=25I.

exercises.title: Conjugate pair
exercises.prompt: A real matrix has eigenvalue 2+3i. Which other eigenvalue is guaranteed?
exercises.explanation: Conjugating Av=lambda v for a real A gives A conjugate(v)=conjugate(lambda) conjugate(v).

exercises.title: Diagonal trajectory
exercises.prompt: For x_(k+1)=diag(2,1/2)x_k and x_0=(3,8), find the first coordinate of x_3.
exercises.explanation: The first coordinate is 3*2^k, so at k=3 it is 24.

exercises.title: Stable and unstable directions
exercises.prompt: Classify the origin for x_(k+1)=diag(2,1/3)x_k and describe the exceptional initial states that still converge to zero.
exercises.explanation: The origin is a saddle. The first coordinate expands by 2 and the second contracts by 1/3. Exactly the states on the y-axis, with first coordinate zero, converge to the origin.

exercises.title: A neutral eigenmode
exercises.prompt: For A=[[3/4,1/4],[1/4,3/4]] and x_0=(6,2), find lim x_k where x_(k+1)=Ax_k.
exercises.explanation: The eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1) have eigenvalues 1 and 1/2. Since x_0=4(1,1)+2(1,-1), x_k=4(1,1)+2(1/2)^k(1,-1), tending to (4,4).
rubric: Decompose the initial state in eigenvectors.
Retain the unit-eigenvalue mode and discard the decaying mode in the limit.

exercises.title: Alternating decay
exercises.prompt: Describe the behavior of x_k=(-1/2)^k(2,1) as k tends to infinity.
exercises.explanation: The vectors alternate between opposite directions on the same line while their norms shrink by a factor 1/2 each step. They converge to zero.
rubric: Use the modulus less than 1 to prove decay.

exercises.title: Periodic motion
exercises.prompt: For R=[[0,-1],[1,0]] and x_0=(1,0), what is the smallest positive integer k for which R^k x_0=x_0?
exercises.explanation: Successive states are (0,1),(-1,0),(0,-1),(1,0). Four quarter turns give the first return.

exercises.title: A contracting rotation
exercises.prompt: For A=[[0,-1/2],[1/2,0]], describe the angle and norm change per step and the limit of A^k v for any real vector v.
exercises.explanation: Each step rotates counterclockwise by pi/2 and scales the norm by 1/2. Hence ||A^k v||=2^(-k)||v||, which tends to zero.
rubric: Give a norm formula proving convergence.

topics.name: Inner products and orthogonal projections
topics.description: Compute orthogonal decompositions and connect complements with matrix spaces.

skills.name: Orthogonality and complements
skills.description: Use dot products, norm identities and orthogonal matrices.

skills.name: Projection and distance
skills.description: Find closest vectors in subspaces using orthogonal bases or normal vectors.

lesson.title: Orthogonality simplifies coordinates
paragraphs: For real vectors, u dot v=sum u_i v_i and ||u||=sqrt(u dot u). Orthogonality means dot product zero. An orthogonal set of nonzero vectors is independent: dot a zero linear combination with each vector to isolate its coefficient.

An orthonormal set is orthogonal and has unit lengths. A square matrix Q with orthonormal columns satisfies Q^T Q=I and Q^(-1)=Q^T; it preserves dot products and lengths. Orthogonal columns without normalization do not make a matrix orthogonal.

The orthogonal complement W-perp contains all vectors perpendicular to every member of W. If W has dimension r in R^n, W-perp has dimension n-r. For a real matrix A, (Col A)-perp=Nul(A^T), since A^T z lists the dot products of z with A's columns.

lesson.title: Projection is the closest subspace vector
paragraphs: For nonzero u, projection of y onto span{u} is ((y dot u)/(u dot u))u. With y=(3,1) and u=(1,1), the coefficient is 4/2=2, giving (2,2). The residual (1,-1) is perpendicular to the line.

For an orthogonal basis u_j, add these one-dimensional projections. For orthonormal columns assembled into U, the projection matrix is P=UU^T. It satisfies P^2=P and P^T=P. If a supplied basis is not orthogonal, this direct sum formula is invalid until the basis is orthogonalized.

Write y=p+r with p in W and r perpendicular to W. For any w in W, ||y-w||^2=||r||^2+||p-w||^2, proving p is the unique closest vector. Distance is ||r||, whereas squared distance is r dot r; do not confuse them.

exercises.title: A norm
exercises.prompt: Find the Euclidean norm of (2,-3,6).
exercises.explanation: The squared norm is 4+9+36=49, so the norm is 7.

exercises.title: Choose an orthogonality parameter
exercises.prompt: Find t so that (1,2,-1) is orthogonal to (t,1,4).
exercises.explanation: The dot product is t+2-4=t-2, which vanishes at t=2.

exercises.title: Orthogonal complement of a plane
exercises.prompt: Find a basis for W-perp where W={(x,y,z):x+2y-2z=0}.
exercises.explanation: The plane's normal is n=(1,2,-2). W is two-dimensional, so W-perp is one-dimensional and has basis {(1,2,-2)}.
rubric: Explain that it spans the entire complement.

exercises.title: Orthogonal matrix inverse
exercises.prompt: Find the inverse of Q=[[0,-1],[1,0]] using orthogonality.
exercises.explanation: Its columns are orthonormal, so Q^(-1)=Q^T=[[0,1],[-1,0]].
rubric: Check orthonormal columns or Q^T Q=I.

exercises.title: Project onto a line
exercises.prompt: Project y=(4,2) orthogonally onto span{(1,1)}.
exercises.explanation: The coefficient is (4+2)/(1+1)=3, so the projection is (3,3). The residual (1,-1) is orthogonal to (1,1).
rubric: Divide by the squared norm, not the norm.
Give the vector projection and verify the residual.

exercises.title: Distance to a coordinate plane
exercises.prompt: Find the distance from (2,-1,5) to the plane z=0.
exercises.explanation: The projection is (2,-1,0), leaving residual (0,0,5) of length 5.

exercises.title: Projection using a nonunit normal
exercises.prompt: Project y=(3,0,0) onto the plane x+y+z=0.
exercises.explanation: Subtract the component along n=(1,1,1): proj_n(y)=(3/3)n=(1,1,1). The plane projection is (2,-1,-1). Its coordinates sum to zero and the residual is normal to the plane.
rubric: Subtract the normal projection from y.
Check plane membership and orthogonal residual.

exercises.title: Projection matrix
exercises.prompt: Find the standard matrix of orthogonal projection onto span{(1,1)} in R^2.
exercises.explanation: Normalize u=(1,1)/sqrt(2). Then P=uu^T=(1/2)[[1,1],[1,1]].
rubric: Use a unit vector or divide uu^T by u^T u.

exercises.title: Complement dimension
exercises.prompt: A subspace W of R^7 has dimension 3. Find dim(W-perp).
exercises.explanation: The dimensions of a subspace and its orthogonal complement sum to the ambient dimension: 7-3=4.

exercises.title: Pythagoras proves best approximation
exercises.prompt: Let W be a linear subspace of Euclidean space. Suppose y=p+r with p in W and r in W-perp. Prove p is the unique closest vector to y in W in the Euclidean norm.
exercises.explanation: For any w in W, p-w is in W and is perpendicular to r. Thus ||y-w||^2=||r||^2+||p-w||^2>=||r||^2=||y-p||^2. Equality occurs exactly when p-w=0, hence w=p.
rubric: Establish the perpendicular decomposition for arbitrary w.
Apply Pythagoras and state the equality condition.

topics.name: Gram-Schmidt and least squares
topics.description: Orthogonalize bases and fit inconsistent data using normal equations.

skills.name: Gram-Schmidt
skills.description: Subtract projections onto previously obtained orthogonal directions.

skills.name: Least-squares models
skills.description: Form normal equations, compute fits and distinguish unique fitted vectors from unique coefficients.

lesson.title: Remove the components already accounted for
paragraphs: Gram-Schmidt turns an independent list into an orthogonal list spanning the same subspaces at each stage. Start u_1=v_1. Then u_2=v_2-proj_(u_1)(v_2), and at later stages subtract projections onto every earlier u_j. Normalize only after removing all earlier components.

For v_1=(1,1,0), v_2=(1,0,1), the projection coefficient is 1/2, so u_2=(1/2,-1/2,1). Multiplying by 2 gives the simpler orthogonal direction (1,-1,2). An orthonormal basis is (1,1,0)/sqrt(2) and (1,-1,2)/sqrt(6).

A zero residual means the new vector lies in the span of earlier vectors. It cannot be normalized. For an independent input list this does not occur in exact arithmetic. This course treats Gram-Schmidt directly without adding QR factorization beyond the supplied scope.

lesson.title: Least squares fits the attainable part
paragraphs: When Ax=b is inconsistent, minimize ||b-Ax||. The fitted vector A x_hat is the projection of b onto Col(A), so the residual must be perpendicular to every column. This gives the normal equations A^T A x_hat=A^T b.

If A has independent columns, A^T A is invertible and the coefficient vector is unique. If its columns are dependent, the best fitted vector is still unique but multiple coefficients can represent it. The least-squares error is the residual norm, while the objective is often written as its square; they have the same minimizers.

To fit y=beta_0+beta_1 t to data, place [1,t_i] in each row of the design matrix and y_i in the target vector. For points (-1,1),(0,0),(1,1), the columns are orthogonal; the normal equations give beta_0=2/3 and beta_1=0. The fitted constant is the mean, and the residual sums to zero.

exercises.title: One Gram-Schmidt subtraction
exercises.prompt: Apply Gram-Schmidt to v1=(1,1,0), v2=(1,0,1). Give an orthogonal basis for their span; normalization is not required.
exercises.explanation: Keep u1=(1,1,0). Subtract half of u1 from v2 to get (1/2,-1/2,1); rescale it to (1,-1,2). The resulting two vectors are orthogonal and span the original plane.
rubric: Give nonzero perpendicular vectors with the same span.

exercises.title: Normalize an orthogonal basis
exercises.prompt: Normalize the orthogonal vectors (1,1,0) and (1,-1,2).
exercises.explanation: Their norms are sqrt(2) and sqrt(6). Divide each vector by its own norm, giving (1,1,0)/sqrt(2) and (1,-1,2)/sqrt(6).
rubric: Retain orthogonality and achieve unit lengths.

exercises.title: Detect dependent input
exercises.prompt: Gram-Schmidt starts with v1=(1,2) and v2=(2,4). What goes wrong at the second normalization, and why?
exercises.explanation: v2 is twice v1, so subtracting its projection leaves zero. Zero has no unit normalization; the input list is dependent and its span has dimension one.
rubric: Calculate or identify the zero residual.
Relate it to input dependence rather than a formula failure.

exercises.title: Third Gram-Schmidt direction
exercises.prompt: An orthogonal list is u1=(1,1,0), u2=(1,-1,0). Orthogonalize v3=(2,0,3) against both and give the residual's third coordinate.
exercises.explanation: Both projection coefficients equal 1. Subtracting u1+u2=(2,0,0) leaves (0,0,3).

exercises.title: Fit one coefficient
exercises.prompt: Find the least-squares scalar x for A=(1,1,1)^T and b=(1,4,7)^T.
exercises.explanation: The normal equation is 3x=1+4+7=12, so x=4, the data mean.

exercises.title: Squared residual error
exercises.prompt: For A=(1,1,1)^T, b=(1,4,7)^T and best-fit scalar x=4, compute ||b-Ax||^2.
exercises.explanation: The residual is (-3,0,3), whose squared norm is 9+0+9=18. The norm itself would be sqrt(18).

exercises.title: Form and solve normal equations
exercises.prompt: Find the least-squares solution for A=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]] and b=(1,1,4).
exercises.explanation: A^T A=[[2,1],[1,2]] and A^T b=(5,5). Solving gives x_hat=(5/3,5/3). The residual (-2/3,-2/3,2/3) is orthogonal to both columns.
rubric: Build the correct normal matrix and target.
Solve for both coefficients and check the residual.

exercises.title: Fit a line
exercises.prompt: Find the least-squares line y=a+bt through data (-1,1),(0,2),(1,5).
exercises.explanation: The design columns are (1,1,1) and (-1,0,1), which are orthogonal. Normal equations give 3a=8 and 2b=4, hence y=8/3+2t.
rubric: Use a design matrix with columns 1 and t.

exercises.title: Nonunique coefficients, unique fit
exercises.prompt: Find all least-squares solutions for A=[[1,1],[1,1]] and b=(1,3). Explain whether the fitted vector is unique.
exercises.explanation: Every output is (s,s) with s=x1+x2. The best s is 2, so all solutions satisfy x1+x2=2, or (x1,x2)=(2-t,t). The fitted vector is uniquely (2,2), although its coefficients are not unique.
rubric: Distinguish the two forms of uniqueness.

exercises.title: Why the normal matrix is invertible
exercises.prompt: Prove that a real matrix A with independent columns has invertible A^T A.
exercises.explanation: If A^T A x=0, multiply by x^T to obtain ||Ax||^2=0, hence Ax=0. Column independence forces x=0. The square matrix A^T A has trivial null space and is therefore invertible.
rubric: Invoke column independence and the square invertibility criterion.

topics.name: Symmetric matrices and academic reasoning
topics.description: Construct orthogonal eigenbases and prove or refute statements with all hypotheses checked.

skills.name: Spectral theorem
skills.description: Use real eigenvalues, perpendicular eigenspaces and orthogonal diagonalization.

skills.name: Proofs and counterexamples
skills.description: Verify hypotheses and establish or refute a universal matrix claim.

lesson.title: Symmetry gives an orthonormal eigenbasis
paragraphs: A real square matrix is symmetric when A^T=A. The spectral theorem says it has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so A=QDQ^T with Q orthogonal and D real diagonal. Symmetric and orthogonal are different properties: diag(2,3) is symmetric but does not preserve lengths.

For A=[[3,1],[1,3]], eigenvalues are 4 and 2, with eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1). Normalize each by sqrt(2), place them in Q in that order, and set D=diag(4,2). The identity Q^T A Q=D verifies the chosen ordering.

Eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are perpendicular: lambda u^T v=(Au)^T v=u^T Av=mu u^T v. If lambda!=mu, the dot product is zero. Inside a repeated eigenspace, choose an orthonormal basis using Gram-Schmidt.

lesson.title: A mathematical claim needs a complete argument
paragraphs: To prove a universal statement, start with arbitrary objects satisfying its assumptions and derive its conclusion. A numerical example can illustrate a true statement but cannot prove it. To refute one, a single explicit counterexample is enough only after all assumptions and the failed conclusion have been checked.

The claim that row equivalence preserves diagonalizability is false. The invertible Jordan matrix [[1,1],[0,1]] is row equivalent to I, but its eigenspace has dimension one and it cannot diagonalize. This separates row operations from similarity.

Projection identities provide useful proof exercises. If P^2=P and Pv=lambda v with v!=0, then lambda^2 v=lambda v, so lambda is 0 or 1. To conclude that an idempotent matrix is an orthogonal projection, symmetry is also needed; idempotence alone can describe an oblique projection.

exercises.title: Symmetric versus orthogonal
exercises.prompt: Is diag(2,-3) symmetric, orthogonal, both or neither? Explain.
exercises.explanation: It is symmetric since it equals its transpose. It is not orthogonal because A^T A=diag(4,9), not I.

exercises.title: Orthogonal diagonalization
exercises.prompt: Give an orthogonal diagonalization of A=[[3,1],[1,3]].
exercises.explanation: Take Q=(1/sqrt(2))[[1,1],[1,-1]] and D=diag(4,2). Its columns are unit eigenvectors for 4 and 2, so A=QDQ^T.

exercises.title: Distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal
exercises.prompt: Prove that eigenvectors of a real symmetric matrix corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
exercises.explanation: Let Au=lambda u and Av=mu v. Symmetry gives lambda u^T v=(Au)^T v=u^T Av=mu u^T v. Since lambda-mu is nonzero, u^T v=0.
rubric: Use symmetry to move A across the dot product.
Use distinct eigenvalues to conclude a zero dot product.

exercises.title: Orthogonal diagonalization implies symmetry
exercises.prompt: Prove that a real matrix A=QDQ^T with Q orthogonal and D real diagonal is symmetric.
exercises.explanation: A^T=(QDQ^T)^T=QD^T Q^T=QDQ^T=A because D^T=D.
rubric: Use symmetry of a real diagonal matrix.

exercises.title: Idempotent eigenvalues
exercises.prompt: Prove that every eigenvalue of a matrix P satisfying P^2=P is either 0 or 1.
exercises.explanation: For a nonzero eigenvector v, P^2v=lambda^2v and Pv=lambda v. Idempotence gives lambda(lambda-1)v=0. Since v is nonzero, lambda=0 or 1.
rubric: Apply the identity to an eigenvector.
Use its nonzero status to derive the scalar equation.

exercises.title: Row equivalence does not preserve eigenstructure
exercises.prompt: Refute: if A is row equivalent to a diagonalizable matrix B, then A is diagonalizable.
exercises.explanation: Take A=[[1,1],[0,1]] and B=I_2. Subtract row 2 from row 1 to reduce A to B, so they are row equivalent. B is diagonal, but A has only one independent eigenvector for its double eigenvalue 1.
rubric: Verify diagonalizability of B and failure for A.

exercises.title: Norm equality forces perpendicularity
exercises.prompt: For real vectors u,v, prove that ||u+v||=||u-v|| implies u dot v=0.
exercises.explanation: Square both nonnegative norms and expand. The left side is ||u||^2+2u dot v+||v||^2 and the right side has -2u dot v instead. Equality gives 4u dot v=0.
rubric: Cancel matching terms and derive orthogonality.

exercises.title: Product of diagonalizable matrices
exercises.prompt: Refute: the product of two diagonalizable real matrices must be diagonalizable. Verify every part of your counterexample.
exercises.explanation: Let A=[[1,1],[0,2]] and B=diag(2,1). Each has distinct real eigenvalues 1 and 2, hence is diagonalizable. Their product is [[2,1],[0,2]], whose sole eigenvalue 2 has a one-dimensional eigenspace, so it is not diagonalizable.
rubric: Show its geometric multiplicity is insufficient.

exercises.title: A symmetric square has nonnegative eigenvalues
exercises.prompt: Let A be real symmetric. Prove every eigenvalue of A^2 is nonnegative.
exercises.explanation: Write A=QDQ^T by the spectral theorem with real diagonal entries d_j. Then A^2=QD^2Q^T. Its eigenvalues are d_j^2, all nonnegative.
rubric: Use an orthogonal diagonalization with real entries.
Square it correctly and identify the new eigenvalues.

exercises.title: Idempotent need not mean orthogonal projection
exercises.prompt: For P=[[1,1],[0,0]], verify P^2=P and explain why P is not an orthogonal projection.
exercises.explanation: Direct multiplication gives P^2=P. It is not symmetric. More concretely, y=(0,1) maps to (1,0), and residual y-Py=(-1,1) has nonzero dot product -1 with the image direction (1,0). Thus the projection is oblique, not orthogonal.
rubric: Show symmetry fails or exhibit a nonorthogonal residual.
